title: Sita's question about the bow
hookLine: before Rama meets Agastya, Sita asks whether he should carry weapons at all: ahimsa and the protector's bow
carry: ahimsa, and a bow carried only to protect

lines: WHAT WEAPONS DO TO THEIR BEARER.
cards: They're walking between hermitages, Rama ahead with his bow, Sita in the middle, Lakshmana behind. The path is narrow, the trees close, and nobody has spoken for a while. Then Sita, quietly, starts to talk.
She's been thinking about that promise. She doesn't doubt Rama's goodness. She's worried about something else.
You vowed to kill the rakshasas, and they haven't done anything to you. I'm afraid of what weapons do to the person who carries them.

teach.b: She lays out her worry carefully. Three faults come from desire, she says: speaking falsely, wanting someone else's wife, and violence without enmity, harming those who haven't harmed you. You've never done the first two.
The third worries me. Then she tells a story.
Once Indra, uneasy at an ascetic's power, came disguised as a warrior and left a sword with him for safekeeping.
The ascetic carried it everywhere, to gather fruit, to bathe, to pray, and slowly, without noticing, he grew rough, then cruel, and lost his practice. Fire, she says, is kindled by being near fuel.
I only say this out of love. Rama's answer is just as tender. You say this because you care for me.
But a warrior carries a bow so that no one in distress cries out unheard. The sages came to me for refuge, and I gave my word.
Hindus have a name for what Sita is guarding: ahimsa, not harming. It comes first in yoga's list of restraints, and it's a big reason many Hindus eat vegetarian.
And Rama names the other half: dharma can ask you to protect. That's why gods on a Hindu altar hold weapons in some hands and bless with another.
Many teachers read those weapons as guarding dharma, never harming the innocent.
The text lets both speak. Then ten years pass in the hermitages of Dandaka, and the road leads to Agastya.

how: Reciters give Sita's question about weapons in the Aranya Kanda its full length, and Hindu teachers who discuss it note that the text lets both her concern and Rama's answer stand.

o: the bow Rama breaks to win Sita at Janaka's court
a sage's gifts, after Sita asks what weapons do to us
weapons Lakshmana forges for the war on Lanka

p: left with an ascetic, who grew cruel
not harming: what Sita is guarding
so no one in distress cries out unheard

s: ahimsa means a Hindu may never protect anyone by force
Sita guards ahimsa, and Rama answers that dharma can ask a warrior to protect those who cry out.
in Sita's story, Indra leaves a sword with an ascetic
carrying it everywhere slowly makes him cruel.
ten years pass in the hermitages before Rama reaches Agastya
the text says Rama spends ten years among the sages.

games.q: you're Rama. Sita, out of love, asks you to set aside your vow to fight the rakshasas while in the forest. what do you say?
o: you're right, I'll give up the vow.
I gave my word to the sages; I can't take it back.
games.why: Rama honors her concern, but a promise to those who sought refuge is one he can't break. the text keeps both: ahimsa, and the protector's bow.

practice: Many Hindus close a prayer with Om shanti, shanti, shanti: peace, three times. Let your hands rest empty in your lap, as if you'd set down the ascetic's sword.
If you pray, say it slowly, once for yourself, once for the people near you, once for the world. If you don't, breathe out peace three times, for the same three.

wordCard.voice: Agastya's weapons. Before the sage gives Rama weapons, Sita asks whether carrying them will change him, and Rama answers with his promise.

orig.note: Sanskrit agastya: the great sage of the south, whom Rama meets next.

carryVoice: Your line: ahimsa, and a bow carried only to protect. Sita said it out of love, and Rama heard it that way. Day five hundred fifty-seven, done.
